item.title: From "paper car" to pole – What changed for Verstappen and Red Bull?
AL Division Series Game 1 Preview: New York Yankees @ Tampa Bay Rays
item.author: Estevão Maximo
item.content:encoded: Sweeping the Red Sox with two blowout wins was a joyous occasion, not to mention the tangible positive impact of setting up your rotation for the ALDS. The Yankees can begin the series against the Rays with Gerrit Cole as the Game 1 starter, which is only fitting considering Cole’s regular-season campaign in 2026 began and ended against the Rays, both times with a quality start.Making his postseason debut this season, Cole will get the ball after nearly a week and a half off, his longest time between starts since returning from injury. In three appearances against the AL East champs in the regular season—the most he had against any single team—Cole averaged six innings and delivered a 2.50 ERA, enjoying success against a team not known for its home run pedigree.Having last played a competitive meaningful game well before the end of the regular season, the Rays will set out to prove there is no rust in their game with Drew Rasmussen starting Game 1. Who better to represent what the Rays are all about than Rasmussen, acquired for the power-hitting Willy Adames as a swingman/backend starter, only to turn into one of the more dominant starters in the AL?The postseason scenario and all that it entails could be seen as an opportunity to test the Rays’ resolve when it comes to their ace. Rasmussen was already dominant last season—part of what held him back from entering the conversation with the big boys was just how carefully managed he was by the Rays, who only let him reach or surpass 90 pitches twice in 2025. This year, Rasmussen has done that 17 times, including a career-high 114 pitches in a win over the Yankees just a couple of weeks ago—one in which perhaps the Rays gave a sign of their intentions with a trial run. With this extra leeway, Rasmussen managed to pitch 22 more innings than last season despite having one fewer start (31 to 30).Rasmussen’s ability to go deeper into games than what we’re accustomed to seeing not only from him but also from the Rays as a team is of great value—especially if we are to read into regular season numbers. As much as the Yankees may have a better rotation, perhaps the biggest advantage in this series is in the bullpen. While New York had the second-lowest bullpen ERA in baseball, Tampa was only number 14. The key here, particularly looking at the postseason and a matchup with the Yankees lineup, is that the 95 home runs allowed by the Rays’ bullpen represented the third-highest mark in the bigs.Then again, this is a Tampa team with the benefit of off-days between each of the first three games. One can only imagine how aggressive they might be willing to go with the likes of Bryan Baker, Cam Booser, and Kevin Kelly. While Baker is the closer, Booser gets the nod as the X-factor for the Rays in Game 1 and this series as a whole—the Yankees were 1-for-10 against him in the regular season, the one being an Austin Wells home run.Booser’s importance stems from a complete lack of southpaw options for a team whose only other left-hander who finished the season on the active roster was Steven Matz. Garrett Cleavinger was cleared to be a part of the ALDS roster, but his 2026 numbers were quite bad, with an 89 ERA+ in 41.1 innings.Unlike the Red Sox, all the Rays’ top starters are right-handers, allowing Aaron Boone to utilize his lefty-heavy lineup without fear, starting in Game 1 against Rasmussen. And if Booser can’t shut them down out of the bullpen, Tampa all of a sudden has an incredibly difficult mission to contain Ben Rice, Cody Bellinger, Luis García Jr., and company.

item.title: Giro dell'Emilia Internazionale Donne Elite: Alessia Vigilia takes surprise breakaway win
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Alessia Vigilia sprung a surprise at the Giro dell’Emilia Donne on Saturday, the UNO-X Mobility rider taking a solo victory after attacking the peloton early in the race.Sarah Van Dam (Visma-Lease a Bike) took second place six seconds down, while Lauren Dickson (FDJ United-SUEZ) was third, 14 seconds behind the solo winner.The victory was only the third of the 27-year-old’s career, and the first in three years. It’s certainly the most prestigious, her previous successes coming in .2, fourth-tier events.Vigilia made her move, attacking an eight-rider breakaway with 40 kilometres to go, after her teammate Francesca Pellegrini had buried herself for her team leader. The rider from Bolzano powered away solo, pushing her gap to over five minutes on the chase group, but her lead was reduced to slightly over two minutes as she crested San Luca for the first time. Behind her, a group of around 20 riders closed the gap thanks to a push from Visma-Lease a Bike, but Vigilia crossed the finish line alone and claimed her first victory since 2023.For its 13th edition, this second-tier ProSeries one-day race tackled 111.3km, starting in Ferrara and finishing in Bologna, on the famous San Luca climb, after crossing the finish line at the top of the ascent with only the final 10km to go.Other than the final, the course was largely flat, a short climb to Botteghino coming with 80km the day’s first obstacle, and the peloton stayed together for the opening kilometres. item.title: Mercedes' upgrade letdown - What we know
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: Mercedes is scrambling to understand why its upgrade appears to have taken it backwards rather than forwards at Formula 1’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.Dominant 2026 championship leader Mercedes suffered its "toughest Saturday" of the season at Sepang, with Kimi Antonelli and George Russell fourth and eighth, half a second adrift of Max Verstappen’s polesitting Red Bull.That’s despite Mercedes introducing a major car upgrade that pre-event simulations predicted would bring a laptime improvement of around three tenths.“You're expecting 0.3s gain to kick in and it looks like 0.3s or 0.4s or 0.5s backwards,” Toto Wolff told Sky Sports F1.“[It’s the] first time we miss out on the top three and by quite a chunk, so... Odd. But I guess we will find a solution.”Mercedes was outside the top three in qualifying in Hungary too, but with a deficit that’s almost half of what it faces at Sepang.So what’s going on? Has the upgrade not delivered as expected, how much is down to the unique characteristics of Sepang and can Mercedes hope for better in the grand prix?Mercedes wasn’t helped by having its toughest Friday of the season so far, as weaknesses that it hasn’t suffered with all year appeared.“We have been a little bit caught out on Friday with some car behaviour that we didn't see all year,” Wolff explained.“But it's very hot and the tarmac is very different to all the tracks. It looked really good in [FP3] we seem to have, at least with Kimi , made a step in understanding. Then qualifying was a little bit back to what we saw before, just no performance.”Asked what that unwanted car behaviour was, Wolff said: “It looks like we are very draggy, because it's the first time that we're losing a lot of time on the straights to especially Max [Verstappen].“Then through the low speed, Turn 2 we are not able to turn the car. There's just too much understeer. So overall things we haven't seen all year.”The data backs that up with Antonelli losing three of the five tenths to Verstappen through the low-speed Turns 1-2 alone in Q3.Mercedes can’t rely on its usual straightline advantage on the back straight and the start/finish straight as Verstappen (blue) gains another two tenths on Antonelli (green) from the run out of the Turn 14 right-hander to the line.“With this new package, obviously the window of the way the car operates is different,” Antonelli said.“We're trying to understand in which window the car performance is best. In the high-speed, our performance has been very strong this weekend, but in the low-speed is where we lacked.“Overall we need to understand why and try to move on and improve.”Is the upgrade actually working?So is the Mercedes upgrade working as expected but being blighted by Sepang’s unique conditions (the aged tarmac, the long radius low-speed corners), or is the upgrade mis-firing versus expectations?“Well, that is the big question mark,” Russell said when that was put to him.“If you could have done a direct back-to-back, it would have been great to know, but that's the challenge of this sport.“If I put the upgrade package on last week [in Baku], even if it was worse, we probably still would have been on pole and we'd have been saying it was fantastic.“Equally, if we had the old car here, maybe the result would have been even worse. So that's the challenge.“As a team, we have yet to have a bad race this whole season and this was clearly a very bad qualifying for us.”Russell had taken pole position by over eight tenths in Baku, the biggest pole margin of the season, but the team always expected Sepang to be tougher because it’s a less favourable circuit for its car.“The whole year whenever we went on tracks like this with very open tarmac, we've always struggled,” Antonelli said.“So is it because of the tarmac and because it's so hot out there? Or is it because maybe we're missing something with the new package? So it's really hard to understand.“But we try to do our best and probably Singapore will give us a better read on the package.”Russell described the track surface as “like driving on gravel” and that’s clearly hurting Mercedes more than other teams.There is an element of qualifying looking worse on paper because Antonelli wasted a set of tyres after a Q2 track limits deletion, which prompted him to run earlier than others in Q3 on a single set of tyres.“I understeered off the track, but I think with a clean qualifying, probably P2, maybe P3 on the road, but not P1,” Antonelli said. “Max was a bit too quick for us today.”But there is still undoubtedly a sense of disappointment at Mercedes about how the upgrade debut has gone with Russell calling it the “toughest Saturday of the year” so far.“All the numbers say it's an improvement, but obviously it's a sport that we need to follow the laptimes and not what the numbers say,” Russell said.“So the numbers look absolutely fine and in line with expectations, but the result wasn't.”Ultimately there isn’t one reason for Mercedes’ struggles, as Wolff said: “There are many factors we will need to take into consideration, and we can’t rule anything out at this stage”.There's only so much Mercedes can do more before the grand prix though with only minor set-up tweaks allowed under the parc ferme rules."I think we have a good opportunity tomorrow starting on the clean side," Antonelli said, and he'll be third because of Isack Hadjar's grid penalty for taking a seventh engine of the year."But I still believe that Red Bull still has the upper edge on pace and Ferrari is very close. But we'll do our best. I think track position is going to be very important."We'll try to manage those tyres the best way as possible. And then try to, if we can fight for the win, great. If we have to settle for P2 or P3, we'll take that."The real challenge for Mercedes will come in the coming days as it bids to understand exactly why it's seemingly gone backwards.And it will need to optimise this new package as rolling back to a previous spec car isn’t really an option, given the older spec parts were very near the end of their life, and producing new versions would take an unplanned bite out of its strict cost cap allowance.

item.title: Drew Rasmussen headlines a deep Rays staff entering ALDS
item.author: Nick Power
item.content:encoded: After a thorough dismantling of the Red Sox in a Wild Card sweep, the Yankees are riding high. Their offense torched Boston’s pitchers, scoring 18 runs on 26 hits and swatting four homers in the two-game set. Next up is another division rival, the 98-win Tampa Bay Rays.Tampa’s starting rotation finished second in the AL to the Yankees in ERA, though they did so in 56 fewer innings and with 176 fewer strikeouts. They’re expected to hand the ball to the perennially-underrated Drew Rasmussen in Game 1. The 31-year-old has posted a sub-3.00 ERA in each of his six seasons with Tampa, though a couple of those have been severely shortened by injury. He made 30 starts this year and tossed a career-high 172 innings, going 16-5 with a 2.67 ERA while leading the league in WHIP (0.913) and K:BB ratio (5.44). He finished the season particularly strong, allowing six runs over his last six starts. Of note, he threw a career-high 114 pitches in his last outing of the season, hinting that Kevin Cash, the notoriously short-leashed Rays skipper, may be looking for his ace to shoulder a larger burden than usual.Like Cam Schlittler, Rasmussen’s top three pitches are all fastballs: a cutter, a four-seamer, and a sinker. All three have been lights-out; opponents hit .205 and slugged .326 against the cutter this season, the best they fared against any of the three. He mixes in a changeup that he threw 354 times without allowing an extra-base hit and, less frequently, a curveball and a sweeper. The only item missing from the two-time All-Star’s portfolio is postseason excellence — he’s made just one playoff start, back in 2021, in which he allowed three runs in two innings before getting the hook.Cash has remained noncommittal on how he’ll deploy the rest of his pitching staff. Freddy Peralta, Nick Martinez, Griffin Jax, and Ian Seymour were Rasmussen’s rotation-mates and all are expected to feature in some capacity. After a nightmare first half with the Mets, Peralta rebounded nicely with the Rays. The right-hander went 5-0 with a microscopic 0.79 ERA over his last six starts of the year, earning AL Pitcher of the Month honors for September while regaining the form that saw him finish fifth in NL Cy Young voting last year and firmly entrenching himself in the playoff picture.Martinez was one of the best value signings of the offseason, winning 15 games along with a 3.10 ERA on a one-year, $9 million deal. The 36-year-old faded a bit down the stretch, allowing 20 runs in 42 innings across his last eight starts, and it’s fair to wonder if his career-high 180 innings have caught up with him. The Rays converted Jax from a reliever to a starter midseason and the results were strong. He had a lower ERA in the rotation (3.14) than in the bullpen (8.00) but threw 75 pitches or more in just six of his 23 starts. None of those came in his five September appearances, meaning he’d likely be used more as a bulk arm than a true starter if he does get an October start. Seymour also began the year in the bullpen, though he topped 90 pitches six times after moving to the rotation. He’s the only southpaw of the bunch, a fact which could either make him an attracting starting option or a valuable multi-inning reliever against a Yankees lineup featuring a bevy of lefties. So, too, does the fact that he faced the Bombers in his final start of the season and shoved, holding them to one baserunner in five scoreless innings.With the addition of a superfluous starter or two, the Rays’ bullpen will be a deep, veteran group. Bryan Baker is the team’s shutdown closer, posting a 1.44 ERA that trailed only Toronto’s Louis Varland among qualified relievers while tying for the MLB lead with 41 saves. His .203 BABIP is an outlier, though, suggesting some confluence of good luck and playing into a defense that graded out as the best in the AL by DRS. The last time Baker blew a save was back on May 13th. He relies primarily on a four-seamer against which opponents hit .125 with no home runs this season and a changeup that sits more than 10 mph lower.Cash’s top setup option is Kevin Kelly, who appeared in a club-high 71 games. Kelly pitched to a 2.44 ERA on the season but struggled down the stretch, allowing seven runs in his last eight innings of work. Behind those two, the pecking order is less clear. Cam Booser has been the most effective lefty in the ‘pen, recording a sub-2.00 ERA in 41 innings. Fellow southpaws Garrett Cleavinger and Steven Matz had down years after strong 2025s, as did right-hander Cole Sulser. Casey Legumina is another righty option, as is Tyler Wells, who allowed three earned runs in 18 innings after coming over from Baltimore at the trade deadline. Wells and Cleavinger ended the season on the IL with forearm tightness but each pitched an inning in a scrimmage Tuesday and could be in play. Tampa’s bullpen ERA of 3.99 is more middle-of-the-pack than the performance of its starters, but they still have clear lanes to get through the late innings.In looking at the Rays’ pitching corps as a whole, Rasmussen looms large as their greatest differentiator. He’s a tough matchup for any team, but if the Yankees can get to him tonight with their third starter on the hill, they’ll do a great deal to puncture the Rays’ confidence and derail their winning formula. After Game 1, the Yankees will likely need to contend with a kitchen sink approach from Cash, who can be expected to make aggressive, matchup-based moves to put his pitchers in positions to succeed.

item.title: UEC European Championships: Elias Dybing wins the men junior road race for Norway
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Norway’s Elias Dybing won the junior men’s race at the UEC European Championships in Slovenia on Saturday, the 18-year-old breaking clear on the final ascent of the race’s signature climb to Možjanča.Staying away for the last 15km of the 110.5km race, Dybing held off Aitor Martínez (Spain), who took second place, out-sprinting Jop van den Biggelaar (Netherlands), the pair five seconds ahead of a large group of chasers.The race took place over five laps of a 22km circuit, starting and finishing in the town of Šenčur, each including the challenging climb to Možjanca, which featured gradients of more than 15%.After an opening phase punctuated by several breakaway attempts, one move came from Slovenian Gal Stare, who attacked his breakaway companions on the climb to Možjanca. He quickly opened a gap of more than a minute with around 50 kilometres remaining.Stare was caught 30 kilometres later, and a group of nine riders formed at the front, approaching the final ascent of Možjanca with a lead of more than 40 seconds.Dybing only needed to attack once, his move instantly gapped Martínez and gradually built his advantage. The Spaniard, meanwhile, eventually slipped back into a group of five, though as the peloton closed in, he and Van den Biggelaar escaped to sweep up the remaining medals.Jop Van Den Biggelaar (Ned)Sindre Orholm-Løsseth (Nor)Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Winners and losers from shock Malaysia F1 qualifying
item.author: The Race Team
item.content:encoded: Red Bull catapulting to the top of the order for its first pole of the year, the first for a non-Mercedes powered car in 2026, grabbed the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia headlines.And that makes our winners and losers feature even more of a goldmine, as we assess the best and worst performances of the day.Loser: Mercedes (4th & 8th)This was Mercedes’ worst qualifying performance since Hungary, where Kimi Antonelli was fourth and George Russell seventh, and the temptation is to conclude the substantial upgrade Mercedes brought to Malaysia isn’t working.Team boss Toto Wolff told Sky Sports F1 that Mercedes "still believe the upgrade works" but will need to comb through the data after discovering the car "looks like we are very draggy"."It’s the first time that we're losing a lot of time on the straights, to especially Max," Wolff added. “And then through the low speed, Turn 2, we are not able to turn the car. There's just too much understeer. So overall things we haven't seen all year."Both Russell and Antonelli pointed to the "abrasiveness of the tarmac" (Russell’s words) making Sepang an outlier circuit, with Antonelli suggesting "the whole year, whenever we went on tracks like this with very open tarmac, we've always struggled."So is it because of the tarmac and because it's so hot out there? Or is it because maybe we're missing something with the new package?"Mercedes is a bit stuck right now, because it definitely feels the upgrade has improved the car in high-speed corners, as it was designed to do, but that seems to have come at the cost of its previous strengths through low-speed corners and in straight-line efficiency.And now the cars are in parc ferme after qualifying, there’s no going back unless you want to start from the pitlane, and in any case the old parts were reaching the end of their natural life, so under the cost cap Mercedes can't afford to revert and needs to find a way to make this work."All the numbers say it's an improvement," said Russell. "But obviously it's a sport that we need to follow the laptimes and not what the numbers say."The numbers look absolutely fine and in line with expectations, but the result wasn’t." Winner: Max Verstappen (1st)Nine years on, Max Verstappen and Red Bull are still the quickest combination around Sepang and who’d bet against him in the race?Having not been on pole position all season, Verstappen looked relatively comfortable throughout qualifying, topping each session and taking pole with a three-tenth margin.Team-mate Isack Hadjar completed a strong day for Red Bull (even if he’ll go back five places on the grid), but Verstappen’s four-tenth margin over him shows the difference the four-time world champion made. Winner: Aston Martin (12th & 14th)Easily Aston Martin-Honda’s best performance of the season so far, combining the lighter B-spec car first introduced in Hungary with Honda’s ADUO 2 upgraded engine - which doesn’t seem to be a giant leap but is at least not penalising the car to quite the extent Honda’s engine has been doing so far in 2026.Alonso was just over four tenths away from making Q3, while Lance Stroll - who felt the car "clicked for me during the second push lap in Q1 and came together much better" - was only two places and 0.346s further back, and might have done better but for some scruffy driving in Q2.In a piece of signature Alonso hyperbole, he called it a "miracle that we are fighting with cars that are much faster than us"."No doubts our best weekend in terms of car performance," and "definitely a step forward in terms of competitiveness," Alonso also said."The car is exactly the same as the last four rounds, since Budapest, so it’s just telling us that it depends on the circuit layout and the amount of straights we have, we can be more or less competitive."Although it should be said he expects to go backwards not forwards on Sunday, owing to the aforementioned "miracle" and "some fast cars starting behind us with some penalties as well that tomorrow they will come strong".Winner: Lewis Hamilton (2nd)Ferrari’s qualifying execution has been a consistent bugbear for Lewis Hamilton for much of his time at the team, but Hamilton called Ferrari's Malaysia timing "perfect".He said he was surprised to be on the front row for the first time since Barcelona, having been looking at the third row pre-qualifying."These cars are so sensitive; you make the smallest change and it’s ridiculous the difference it can make from one run, one session to the other," Hamilton said."One click of front wing or one millimetre ride height, a quarter degree of camber, 0.1 of toe, something like that. These little things make such a big difference to balance, it’s literally a moving target that you’re trying to work around, with set-up and also the controls we have."Even understanding throttle application, if you get to full throttle too early here, your stair [ramp down] starts early and you lose time down the straights. These things that I don’t think many of us like."Mastering all of that together is a massive challenge. We’re so on the edge because we’re losing so much on the straights." Winner: Gabriel Bortoleto (10th)His Audi team-mate went out in Q1 and he made it all the way through to Q3, so Gabriel Bortoleto can sleep well knowing he had a good day.The Audi squad looked like it went backwards in Baku, despite its massive upgrade package, but thanks to soul-searching and "long nights" at the factory, it appears to be unlocking some of that new performance.That, plus what Bortoleto described as "when you do very good laps and the car is in a good window and you feel comfortable, you can sometimes do something great".Self-proclaimed "greatness" can be jarring, but its hard to deny Bortoleto a dose of that today. Winner: Valtteri Bottas (21st)Valtteri Bottas looked "pretty slow" in Baku by his own admission, so qualifying over three tenths ahead of Cadillac team-mate Sergio Perez in Malaysia was the perfect response.He has the upgraded Ferrari ADUO 2 engine for the first time this weekend, something Perez elected not to run, having used it in Baku, to save the mileage on it for a different track."There is a difference. It's not huge difference, but there is a difference, so it's nice to have it," Bottas said of the engine upgrade.Asked by The Race if he felt like he was back on form after Baku, Bottas said: "Something was definitely off last weekend, we were so far off, but we changed many things and now the car is again back to normal."No issues at all this weekend, so being able to just get to the rhythm, do the set-up work and go from there." Two races with Williams' new upgrade, twice beaten by his team-mate. This wasn't a good day for Alex Albon.While Carlos Sainz said he did better laps than the Baku ones that got him into Q3 and perhaps his best this year, Albon was another victim of running wide at the Turn 14 right-hander that leads onto the back straight.But Albon reckons the team has been "struggling with parts" - quality rather than quantity in this case - and a change for qualifying "made it worse". So perhaps that explains the deficit between the pair."If we need to do a pitlane start tomorrow [to change the parts], so be it," he added.Loser: Haas (18th and 19th)The worst qualifying result of Haas’s 2026 F1 season comes right off the back of the team’s first double points finish of the year.Esteban Ocon felt he was sent out too early in Q1, so he missed the best of the track conditions, while Ollie Bearman says he was compromised by messy practice sessions, including the wrong set-up being applied to his car."For me, the issue has been an all-weekend long one," Bearman said. “We started out in FP1, it was okay, but then in FP2 we had a problem with the car set-up. "Basically, the set-up that we intended to put on the car was not the set-up that ended up on the car."The car ended up in a state that we would never intend to ever run a race car, not even on an oval."The only time I've actually had a good car and had a good feeling was in that final [qualifying] run."I didn't get everything out of the tyre because it was the first time I had a decent balance all weekend." Loser: Nico Hulkenberg (17th)A big moment at Turn 14 undid Nico Hulkenberg's chances of going any further by 0.087s, out in Q1.That might have been dismissed as normal looking at the team's performance in Baku, but we already know Bortoleto put the car in Q3, so this can only go down as an error that creates an embarrassing qualifying deficit to the only person you can compare Hulkenberg to, his team-mate."Disappointed with myself, didn't put the lap together," was his take.Hulkenberg has a wily way of overturning these set-backs on race day, so don't count him out. Especially as Bortoleto has proven Audi's lack of straight-line speed - which won't improve much for the remainder of the season - won't be the thing that holds Audi back from fighting through the midfield this weekend.

item.author: Madison Pavich
item.content:encoded: Here we go again. After besting the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, the Yankees begin a Division Series matchup against the AL East champions for the second straight year in a row, this time drawing the Rays as opposed to last year’s Blue Jays. The tale of the tape is close between these two teams, the Rays narrowly winning the season series 7-6 after winning the second game of a doubleheader in their four-game series last week. The difference has been where the games have been played, as the Yankees were 2-5 in the Trop but 4-2 against them at Yankee Stadium. Overall the Rays have been the best home team in the league with a 55-26 record, but the Yankees are sending them a challenge as they get to start Gerrit Cole in Game 1 tonight despite having to run out two other aces in the Wild Card, and Cam Schlittler will start Game 2 having pitched to a sterling 1.16 ERA on the road this year. This could easily become a five-game heavyweight bout if the Yankees manage to steal one of these first two games before shifting back to the Bronx, and there’s some revenge on the line for Cole as well after the Rays spoiled his debut season in New York beating them in the 2020 ALDS.We’ve got a lot to get through before gametime, starting with previews abound. Nick and Peter will both dive into the pitchers and hitters respectively that the Yankees have to worry about from Tampa Bay, and Estevao will preview Game 1 specifically as Cole lines up against Drew Rasmussen. The Arizona Fall League gets underway over the weekend as well, and Michael is on hand to go over the Yankees prospects participating. Kento looks back on the saga of Dave Winfield’s career as we celebrate his 75th birthday, and then we’ll be looking ahead to first pitch.American League Division Series Game 1New York Yankees at Tampa Bay RaysTV: TBS/HBO Max, TruTV, UnivisionVenue: Tropicana Field, St. Petersburg, FL1. What are you expecting from Gerrit Cole tonight, and will we see Carlos Rodon used in relief of him?2. Get your picks in for the other Division Series matchups: who wins between the White Sox/Guardians, Braves/Dodgers, and Padres/Brewers?

item.title: Winners and losers from MotoGP's Motegi sprint
item.author: Eden Hannigan
item.content:encoded: Marc Marquez produced a dominant Motegi sprint victory to cut into Jorge Martin’s advantage at the top of the MotoGP riders’ standings to just seven points.After a first-lap pile-up, some surprise podium contenders and two important post-race penalties, here are our winners and losers from the 12-lap sprint. Winner: Marc Marquez (1st) Another sprint win and more points gained in the increasingly yo-yoing championship battle was pretty much the maximum Marquez could take from Saturday. After he missed out on pole to Martin, it was pretty clear another “Marquez strategy” would be deployed - start fast, get the lead at the first corner and not look back, as he’d done in Aragon and Misano. Leaving Martin out to dry on the exit of Turn 1 in what was basically a copy-and-paste from those two races, he marched to victory. He was also very gracious to “one of the most talented riders” he’s ever seen in Diogo Moreira for taking an extra two points away from title rival Martin. After all, every little bit helps.Loser: Alex Marquez (DNF)It’s hard to understand quite what Alex Marquez thought he was going to do when he went steaming into Turn 3, got it all wrong under braking and acted as a bowling ball with an unfortunate Pedro Acosta and Fabio Di Giannantonio the pins. Marquez didn’t do a post-race debrief to explain his side. Instead, he sent a brief voice note via Gresini - saying he felt "so, so sorry” for ruining the race of two riders, as well as his own. Just not a good move, which has rightly been punished.Winner: Diogo Moreira (2nd)Moreira described his podium repeatedly as "not a real result", seemingly to keep expectations in check for Sunday - but, though the Alex Marquez-initiated attrition certainly played a big role, it wasn't at all surprising Moreira was one to benefit.Maybe not faster at Motegi than team-mate Johann Zarco, but seemingly less on edge, he looked a seasoned veteran navigating his way past Marco Bezzecchi and Ai Ogura - and kept his cool on the final lap exiting Turn 10 while the two riders ahead tripped up with track limits.Among the better rides of a really strong rookie season - and please, Honda, announce his 2027 seat already.Loser: Jorge Martin (3rd) Martin was surprisingly calm about the post-race penalty that cost him second place and two points versus Marquez in the title fight, describing it as a “pity” rather than a big deal. Part of that calmness might come from an understanding it could have been worse. Facing tyre problems that forced him into management from mid-race distance, Martin “couldn’t do anything, was just spinning til sixth gear” in the final stages of a sprint he was ultimately relieved to finish.The Aprilia rider stressed it wasn’t an issue of conventional tyre wear but rather overheating at the centre. He was running out of options there - and minus a rear wing, as he was chased down by Moreira and Enea Bastianini on the final lap. Martin was happy with a podium and his overall pace, but some alarm bells may be ringing ahead of the grand prix.Loser: Marco Bezzecchi (6th)The three-bike crash and Martin's track limits slip-up mitigated what could have been a bad championship day for Bezzecchi into just a bad one.Slightly underwhelmed by his performance on the soft rear on Friday, he was tempted by the medium rear after strong pace in morning practice - but it never translated at all in the race.His pace held up, and unlike for other medium-tyre runner Jack Miller there was no blistering - but the peak pace was super-weak, so he got muscled down the order. Martin's example showed the soft rear was precarious - but also that it was the right choice.Honda is best-positioned of any MotoGP manufacturer, obviously, to adjust to any changes to Motegi (a circuit it owns), so it isn't too surprising to see a result like this out of step with the RC213V's recent form.Still, it's very welcome. Honda has been spinning the wheels on its season - Joan Mir sidelined, Luca Marini still struggling to qualify, upgrades non-existent while work is full steam ahead on the 850cc bike - but Moreira's big performance keeps the ennui at bay.The extremely capable stand-in efforts by Somkiat Chantra, too, show that the bike is genuinely delivering the goods.Also doesn't hurt that Honda's big rider signing for 2027 - more on him later - had another very strong day.Loser: Pecco Bagnaia (DNF)Bagnaia shredding the centre of his rear tyre has already had consequences on the wider weekend - with Michelin removing its soft rear tyre from its allocation for the race - but for him it cost a point at best, as he was too limited by grid position anyway.He might be totally faultless in the state of the tyre, but for the last year and a half it feels like he has a worse relationship with the rear Michelin than anyone else within the Ducati camp - so his season-long rear grip struggle probably exacerbated the issue here.Winner: Enea Bastianini (4th)No podium due to track limits - and an instant-classic VAR gesture at the finish to show his discontent.But it's easy to let go of the disappointment given Bastianini has looked the most lively he has in many rounds, as he serves out his Tech3 KTM 'notice period' before pivoting to Trackhouse Aprilia."It has been different and it's very beautiful to be again on top, fighting for something good," he rejoiced - and a long-awaited good qualifying was central to this.Winner: Fabio Quartararo (9th)The Honda-bound Quartararo has been in a really good groove since his extinguished fallout with Yamaha at Aragon - and the trend has continued here.Though his edge over the other Yamahas appears slightly flattered by a very strange day for Jack Miller, who is probably closest on underlying pace, it remains the case that only Quartararo could drag the M1 anywhere near the points here.Attrition obviously helped, but it still took an above-expectations effort to keep the Ducati of Fermin Aldeguer behind.Loser: Brad Binder (18th)“A Saturday to forget” was how Binder summed up his day, and it’s hard to disagree with his assessment as he finished 18th and last of the sprint runners.Binder’s issues were compounded by feeling like he’d “been driven over like a friggin' bus” after a qualifying crash - which saw the mechanics across both KTM garages and Tech3 assemble to get his bike ready in time for the sprint.From there on, it also wasn’t great - with issues at Turn 1 culminating in him riding straight across the gravel due to chatter and locking.

item.title: Michelin makes major Motegi tyre decision after sprint dramas
item.author: Simon Patterson
item.content:encoded: Michelin will remove its softest rear compound from the allocation for Sunday’s Japanese Grand Prix following multiple instances of tyres blistering during Saturday’s half-distance sprint race at Motegi.But it will not, despite lobbying from some teams, make its emergency hard-construction tyre mandatory for the race.It became apparent during the latter stages of the sprint at Motegi that numerous riders were struggling with their rear tyres delaminating, something that was predicted as a possible concern on the newly-resurfaced Motegi asphalt.Pecco Bagnaia was forced to retire from the race with one lap to go, while championship leader Jorge Martin was lucky to hold on to a podium place, finishing the race missing pieces of the rear aerodynamics of his Aprilia after they were shattered by his disintegrating rear tyre.That delamination, a symptom of low wear and high grip that causes a build-up of excess temperatures, was something that Michelin had predicted might be an issue - with the French firm coming prepared with a third rear option using the special construction designed to cope with the high heat that similar tracks like the Red Bull Ring force onto the tyre.“With the new asphalt we never tested here,” Michelin boss Piero Taramasso exclusively told The Race after the sprint. “We know Motegi is a demanding track, and that is why we decided to bring a third rear specification.“In the meeting on Thursday, we already spoke with the riders and the teams, and told them to be careful and to check the temperature of the tyres. It [the soft rear] was at the limit, yesterday and this morning, almost for everyone, but we said 'OK, for 12 laps, we can try it.'“After the sprint, there were three bikes with quite bad blisters. The blistering is when you generate a lot of heat inside the compound. The construction stays intact, but you get bubbles inside the compound and it opens up and makes holes.”It’s believed by The Race’s sources in the paddock that a number of teams subsequently called for Michelin to make the aforementioned hard tyre, brought specifically for this situation, mandatory for Sunday’s race.But these teams have not managed to persuade Michelin to take that step - given that, according to Taramasso, a number of rivals had no issues on Saturday.“We know that in the sprints,” he told The Race, “the riders don’t manage anything, they just go full, so probably the situation tomorrow will be a bit better.“We spoke with Dorna, and the decision for the race is that the rear soft won’t be allowed, and they will have to work with the medium or the hard one. The Michelin suggestion, we really strongly suggest to use the rear hard. That’s why we brought it here, but now it’s up to the teams and the riders to decide.“There are some bikes, like the KTMs, some Hondas, that don’t have the problem. They manage well to not put a lot of energy in the tyres, and we don’t want to penalise them and oblige everyone to go with the hard, even if we suggest it very strongly.”That is likely going to leave a number of teams in something of a dilemma for the main race, though, given that Jack Miller - one of only two riders alongside Marco Bezzecchi to use the medium in the sprint - also experienced similar blistering issues.“We had two mediums on track,” Taramasso added, “and Marco was clean but Jack had some blistering, too. The medium is stronger compared to the soft, but if your bike’s setting is not optimum and you have some more spin, then what you have to do is do everything in your power to limit the spin and put less energy into the rear tyre.”The decision not to make the hard tyre mandatory will come as welcome relief to some, most notably sprint race winner Marc Marquez, whose factory Ducati has struggled all season to use the heat-resistant rear construction, conceding valuable championship points last time out at Austria to the factory Aprilia duo of Martin and Bezzecchi.Given the hard option has been roundly ignored by teams so far in practice this weekend, Sunday's warm-up has been extended from the customary 10 minutes to 20 at Michelin's request, "in order to allow all riders to evaluate" the hard tyre.

item.title: 'I've seen places I never thought I'd go, let alone on a bike' – A year on from the Tour de Langkawi win that sparked British rider Zeb Kyffin's Terengganu twist
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: It was a year ago on stage 7 of Le Tour de Langkawi that Zeb Kyffin roared towards the finish line of Le Tour de Langkawi with local hero Aiman Rosli (Terengganu) and in that winning dash secured not just a victory, but also another contract and another year of pursuing a career in cycling. Before that win the then Unibet Rockets rider hadn't known what was next for the 2026 season, but it turned out that Malaysia provided the answer not just as a venue to throw him into the winner's spotlight so he could secure that much sought contract, but it was also the location that would provide the British rider with his new team."I took my chance when I got it, and I managed my only pro win and looking back on it how special that is so few people actually managed to win a professional bike race," Kyffin told while once again racing at Le Tour de Langkawi in 2026. "I opened my phone when I finished the stage and the manager of this team was like 'well if you wanted the contract we spoke about, here it is' and that was that."This team the he referred to was Terengganu, which, in a curious twist on that key day in Kyffin's career, meant the rider he beat to victory would soon be his teammate at Malaysia's top ranked team, which currently sits fourth in the Asia Tour rankings."I was back in Malaysia in January for the team media week and team launch, and I think only then I realised how big of a setup and how professional of a team it is, and they have that 15-year kind of like history legacy in Asia Tour," said Kyffin."I've been racing full gas since January. I went to India for like the inaugural Pune tour. We went to AlUula Tour after that the Tour of Taiwan, Tour of Hainan, Qinghai, Himalayas. I've seen places I never thought I'd go, let alone on a bike. So it's been quite the year, really."Beyond the experience of racing across a wide variety of previously unknown terrain, there have been top tens and podiums on the results list to show for it, including second overall at the Tour of Shanghai in June among what has been a jam-packed schedule. What the 28-year-old didn't get, however, was much of a chance to sneak off the front unnoticed again as he settled into the new dynamic after two seasons with the Unibet Rockets and five seasons racing with UK-based continental teams. "I kind of got the hang of how it works, and I think it's nice to be on, I guess a smaller team, but also a home team. So we race a lot against the same pros for the whole year," said Kyffin when spoke with him before stage 4. "But then I guess I've also got a bit of a reputation for being the guy who tries to send the long one, and people caught on pretty quickly. So I haven't been able to fly under the radar as much as I probably wanted to. "Like even yesterday, one of the Tudor guys was like, "Save your legs. We'll go together on stage six', and I'm like, 'Oh, for goodness' sake, why does everyone know what I'm going to do?' So I guess it's nice in a way, that you're recognised for what you're capable of. It also ruins the plan a bit."Racing in Asia for a Brit has had its challenges with around 70 race days – his season was also extended by the call-up to race Langkawi as it wasn't initially on his schedule – particularly when it includes a long trip to and from home in Britain plus a change of climates and timezones."I made the most of what I decided to do and I wouldn't trade having seen 15 new countries, or whatever it's been for another year of racing on a club team in Europe or something. It's been exciting."*Cyclingnews attended Le Tour de Langkawi on an invitation/media package from the race that included travel and accommodation. In line with our editorial standards, our coverage is independent and was not subject to review, approval or influence by the organiser or any sponsor; no favourable coverage was promised or given in return.

item.title: Verstappen takes first Red Bull F1 pole of 2026
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: Max Verstappen claimed the first non-Mercedes-powered pole position of the 2026 Formula 1 season so far, while Mercedes suffered its worst qualifying of the year despite debuting upgrades at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.Verstappen topped Q1, Q2 and Q3 at Sepang en route to his first pole position since the 2025 Abu Dhabi title-decider, beating his former title rival Lewis Hamilton by three tenths.Hamilton praised the “perfect timing” of his qualifying run as he claimed his first front row since June's Barcelona Grand Prix, which he won.Isack Hadjar made it two Red Bulls in the top three as the team followed up its strong Baku weekend.But Hadjar won’t start third as he has a five-place grid penalty for taking a seventh internal combustion engine of the season.Kimi Antonelli qualified fourth in the upgraded Mercedes, half a second down on poleman Verstappen running off sync with an earlier final lap after a Q2 track limits penalty set him back and cost a set of tyres, while team-mate George Russell was down in eighth.That’s the weakest qualifying result of Mercedes’ 2026 season so far, eclipsing the fourth and seventh in Hungary in July.Charles Leclerc was fifth ahead of McLaren duo Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.The top 10 was rounded out by Russell, Pierre Gasly’s Alpine and Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto.'Miracle' double Q2 for Aston MartinArvid Lindblad, carrying a back-of-the-grid penalty for taking new engine components this weekend, sacrificed his Q2 to try tow team-mate Liam Lawson into Q3.Lindblad gave Lawson a strong tow on the back straight, but Lawson still ended up two tenths shy of a place in Q3 in 11th.Fernando Alonso was a season’s best 12th for Aston Martin, declaring it a “miracle” afterwards as it’s only his second Q2 appearance of the year.And for the first time this year team-mate Lance Stroll made it through to Q2, lapping only 0.008s slower than Alonso in Q1, before ending up three tenths off Alonso in Q2 in 14th.Carlos Sainz’s Williams split the Aston Martins in 13th place while Franco Colapinto was 15th, having not set a time in Q2 either because of his 15-place grid penalty - five for causing the Baku pile-up and 10 for fresh engine components.Nico Hulkenberg and Alex Albon both made costly errors at the penultimate corner, compromising their final laps and leaving them eliminated in Q1 in 17th and 20th.Haas suffered its first double Q1 exit since Monaco with Ollie Bearman and Esteban Ocon 18th and 19th.Ocon was the first driver to take the chequered flag and told his team “I think we went too early” after his elimination.Valtteri Bottas continued his bounceback from a miserable Azerbaijan Grand Prix, qualifying over three tenths quicker than Cadillac team-mate Sergio Perez - the first time he’s outqualified a team-mate at Sepang in six attempts.1 Max Verstappen (Red Bull Racing) 1m35.130s2 Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari) +0.298s3 Isack Hadjar (Red Bull Racing) +0.428s*4 Kimi item.title: 'The world caves in on you' - Ion Izagirre reflects on broken wrist injury that wrecked end of 17-year career
item.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
item.content:encoded: In any other circumstances for the 37-year-old Basque racer, an accident and injuries suffered on Wednesday when out training would have been a major setback to his plans, but by no means impossible to overcome. But this time round, the broken left wrist that Izagirre ended up with after falling during training has much more serious long-term consequences.In a flash, and barely ten days before Il Lombardia, his plans for a dream farewell to his days as a roadracer at the last Monument of 2026 have all gone up in smoke. That he was in excellent condition - witness his victory at the Memorial Pantani a month back - only makes it all a tougher pill to swallow. But it's the completely wrong-footed ending to his career that is what is perhaps hardest to handle of all."I was out training, doing one of my last rides for the last races of the year," the Cofidis pro told, "and on a downhill that was a bit wet, my back wheel went from underneath me."I was trying to stop myself from going down as I fell and that's when I broke my wrist. It doesn't hurt, and I had a splint put on it at the hospital. But that was that."The injury made it out of the question that he could start the three Italian races he had left on his program as a pro, Coppa Agostini on October 4, Tre Valli Varesine (October 6) and Il Lombardia (October 11) - where he has two top ten places in his career, including a fourth in 2024. As ends of careers go, so close to the finish line, you'd need a heart of stone not to feel that this was a truly harsh twist of fate.What made it worse, the Cofidis racer told was that he was in great condition "and hoping to do something good to round it all off with a good taste, at least give it 100% and finish my career, too, riding a bike, not like this.""But that's how it plays out sometimes. You never want it, never expect it, but sometimes that's just what happens."Il Lombardia clearly is a Classic that suits him, too and after the big boost to his motivation he'd had from winning the Memorial, he was raring to get back into racing one last time."The Italian races I'd done before, I was going well, but I wasn't at the level I wanted, maybe because of the heat or whatever. I couldn't show what I'd got," he said."But then the weather changed; it turned rainier and cooler, and my body really responded, and in Pantani I was always up there, getting in the moves and so on."Then in the last moment, when four of us went ahead, I could play it out well in the sprint. So by then I knew I was on a roll, and it made me feel confident for what was to come."That could hardly have changed more dramatically after his accident on Wednesday, out training alone and building his form one last time. His morale now, he agrees, is that of feeling screwed."Yes, above all yesterday when it all happened. I dunno, I just couldn't believe it. When I couldn't hold the handlebar with my left hand, I realised it was to my season and my career. The world caves in on you."I didn't want to finish my career with a plaster on my wrist. I wanted to finish it enjoying my racing in the Italian races. But it's not going to happen that time."His only way of trying to fight back against the misery is, as he says, that he's received lots of messages of support and sympathy, also reminding him that he's had an exceptionally good last season and to try and focus on that.They're not wrong, either. Apart from Pantani, Izagirre had both been consistent and taken another top-level one-day race, the GP Miguel Indurain, along with a fourth place overall in the Itzulia Basque Country, a seventh in Flèche Wallonne and a sixth in Eschborn-Frankfurt this season. He also raced the Tour de France - a race where he's twice been a stage winner - taking part in breakaways up until the last day in the Alps."But maybe it's a bit too soon to try and feel upbeat," Izagirre said, "instead right now you could say I'm in mourning. It's just a feeling of being hurt and demotivated, disappointed with what happened."Maybe further down the line, looking at things more objectively, I'll value this last season, what I've done in it, a lot more."If road racing is now out of the question - and with it the celebrations and farewell dinner he and the team had planned after Lombardia - he hasn't totally lost hope of perhaps ending the very last chapter of his career as he wanted. That will be a cyclo-cross event held each year on October 25 in his home town of Ormaiztegi in the Basque Country. "There are still 25 days and let's hope that's possible that I recover in time," he said, "maybe that way I'd finish it all off at home.""I've been able to race it in the last few years, which is something that wasn't possible before then because the teams were more worried about the risks of crashes and injuries and so on. "But when I've been able to do it, I've done it, and this year even more so, as it's my last chance. Let's see if I'll be able to do it again, for one last time."After that, what is out of the question, he said, is turning to an alternative career in gravel or cyclo-cross in the future. His only 'career plan' right now is to be with his family and then, he reckons, other ideas will come up. But in terms of racing, as he said, "When I hang up my wheels, that's me done for good. I'll go on riding a bike out of pure pleasure, and as a fan of the sport.""Cycling has given me a lot, and I think it'll help me clear my head if I need it in the future, too, by simply riding the bike. But without any need of being out there doing series, training hard and so on. Just choosing the day and the place and the time and the people I want to be with. It'll be another world."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!

item.title: Alex Marquez gets hefty penalty for multi-bike Motegi crash
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: Gresini Ducati rider Alex Marquez will serve a double long-lap penalty in Sunday's Japanese Grand Prix at Motegi for causing a multi-bike crash in the sprint.Marquez was attacking fellow Ducati rider Fabio Di Giannantonio for sixth place coming into Turn 3 on the opening lap, but ran out of room to navigate the corner as Pedro Acosta cut back in after being forced to the outside by Bastianini.Marquez thus lost the front in trying desperately to slow down, hitting Acosta, before his bike then also collected Di Giannantonio on the outside.He will retain fifth on the grid on Sunday but will be compromised by a double long-lap assessed by the Simon Crafar-led stewards' panel, despite this being a first offence this season for the Gresini man.Incidentally, the crash eliminated Marquez's future KTM team-mate in Di Giannantonio and his future employer's lead rider in Acosta.Other double long-lap penalties this season included one for Joan Mir for ignoring a black-and-orange flag and ones for Jorge Martin and Johann Zarco for causing multi-rider pile-ups at the start.Speaking to media after the sprint, Acosta said that incidents like these happened in racing but semi-chastised Marquez for "trying to get a podium quite early".He also lamented a lost opportunity to make up points on third-placed-in-the-standings Marco Bezzecchi, believing that a podium - though likely not a win - was on the cards had he stayed on.Marquez, meanwhile, said he accepted the penalty and that he had made a mistake, and apologised for ending his rivals' races.

item.title: Nil Gimeno snares first professional win at stage 7 of Le Tour de Langkawi to Batu Pahat
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: Nil Gimeno (Equipo Kern Pharma) took his first professional victory on stage 7 of Le Tour de Langkawi to Batu Pahat, as the break of four prevailed despite a charged pursuit by the sprinters teams.Gimeno, who was a frustrating fourth on stage 4 when the break survived in the Cameron Highlands, wasn't going to let a second opportunity slip him by. This time he got to celebrate rather than commiserate as he crossed the line ahead of Mario Aparicio (Burgos Burpellet-BH) in second and Andrei Stepanov (Wheeltop Rotor Chengdu) in third. The remaining member of the break, Adne van Engelen (Terengganu), was the one who this time had to settle for fourth."We came here for a stage victory," an elated Gimeno, who couldn't get the smile off his face, told reporters after the stage. "I thought it was the best opportunity the fourth day, but it came today, so I'm over the moon."The quartet upset the sprinters plans after going out early as part of a group of seven and it was a hard-earned second break win of the tour. None of the four took the foot off the accelerator pedal until the race was done and Gimeno had claimed the first Spanish stage win of the race, which is in its 30th edition, with an impressive turn of speed."I know I'm really fast, but you never know when you go full gas all the day," said Gimeno. "You don't know if you have the strength in the sprint but luckily, all the riders in the breakaway, we committed ... each one of them went full gas all the way." The final day of racing in stage 8 on Sunday is expected to deliver a sprint showdown, although there is a category 3 climb at 50km to go that once again has some potential to create a tempting launch point for those looking for one last roll of the dice at the Malaysian ProTour race.Lennart Jasch (Tudor Pro Cycling) enters the deciding stage with his grip on the leader's jersey remaining firm as he kept his 26 second gap to Alex Balderstone (Caja Rural-Seguros RGA) intact on stage 7. Jasch claimed the jersey on stage 2, and hasn't put a foot wrong since, but is not prepared to start celebrating a potential GC victory, on his first attempt as leader, just yet."I don't really dare to speak too much about it because today on paper it was an easy day but it was a really hard day so in the end its a bike race like every other day and tomorrow, for sure it won't be easy," said Jasch at the post stage media conference. "There are still a lot of things that can happen."There were 109 riders starting the stage in the historic but vibrant location of Melaka, and sadly one of the missing riders, Ronan Auge (Unibet Rose Rockets) was in hospital after crashing on stage 6, with his squad saying that while his condition is currently stable and not life-threatening he was being "kept in a medically induced coma to optimise his treatment".After the racing started, Aiman Rosli (Terengganu) was the first rider off the mark, determined to get into the break particularly with the first intermediate sprint at his home town, Tangkak, at 45km into the day of racing. Plenty of others, however, had the same idea.There were twists and turns when it came to forming a lead group but by the time the race was 28km in a break of seven had formed which included Mario Aparicio (Burgos Burpellet-BH), Nil Gimeno (Kern Pharma), Santiago Herreño (Bardiani CSF 7 Saber) Adne van Engelen and Kee Zhe Yie of Terengganu, Andrei Stepanov (Wheeltop Rotor Chengdu) and George Matsui (Aisan).Matsui and Kee fell away, making it a group of five with 2:25 to the peloton at 30km to go and then Herreño was next.It was a determined chase from behind but they were only making gradual inroads. No matter what torture the XDS-Astana team and Modern Adventure squad were putting themselves through so Matteo Malucelli and Riley Pickrell could face-off in another sprint, it didn't seem to be enough.They still had more than a kilometre at 35 seconds to go after working together flawlessly to make sure the break survived for a second time at the 2026 edition of Le Tour de Langkawi.*Cyclingnews attended Le Tour de Langkawi on an invitation/media package from the race that included travel and accommodation. In line with our editorial standards, our coverage is independent and was not subject to review, approval or influence by the organiser or any sponsor; no favourable coverage was promised or given in item.title: Thrown in with Giggs and Beckham: how Manchester United tried to get Billy Kenny
item.author: Billy Kenny
item.content:encoded: Former Everton midfielder, known as the ‘Goodison Gazza’, recalls being made to feel special by Alex Ferguson in this autobiography extract “So this is the scouser ya been goin’ on aboot then …” My face turned Manchester United red. Scanning the room full of smiles and staring eyes, I identified the mystery Scottish voice as the man who’d just become the first player to score more than 20 league goals for the club since George Best in the 1960s. “Good answer,” replied Brian McClair after following up on my smile and nod by asking whether I supported Everton or Liverpool. “Ye’ll dee well ’ere laddie.”Brian Kidd had just introduced me to the Man United first team by silencing the room to draw attention to my presence. “Lads, this is Billy from up the road,” he said. I was still starstruck from seeing all these famous faces as my chauffeur for the day, Eric Harrison, pulled up in the car park at The Cliff a few minutes earlier. Paul McGrath. Mark Hughes. Bryan Robson. Kevin Moran. Norman Whiteside. I ticked them all off in my head. Thank fuck I was developing an ear for everyday Glaswegian because after a bit of piss-taking from the first-teamers about being a scouser, I found myself standing in an office at the end of a short and narrow corridor, shaking hands with another one.Continue reading...

item.title: MotoGP Japanese GP: Marquez defeats Moreira for sprint victory
item.content:encoded: Marc Marquez closed the gap to world championship leader Jorge Martin by claiming victory in the sprint race at Motegi on Saturday.Jorge Martin and Enea Bastianini crossed the line second and third but were both demoted a place after the finish for exceeding track limits, giving Moreira his best MotoGP finish.KTM's Pedro Acosta was taken out of the race by Marc's brother Alex on the first ...Keep reading

item.title: Marquez beats penalised Martin in Motegi sprint, Moreira stars
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: Ducati MotoGP rider Marc Marquez took five points out of a penalised Jorge Martin's championship lead with a commanding win in the Motegi sprint.Marquez picked off Martin at the start, setting up the move through Turn 1 and completing it through Turn 2.No real victory battle materialised from there as Marquez established a one-second buffer and managed it from there on out, with Martin looking to settle what should have been - but wasn't - an equally-comfortable second place.Both anyway gained significant ground on outside title hopeful Marco Bezzecchi, who had a very poor race despite being aided by attrition.Three rivals were removed from the podium battle as, after being overtaken into Turn 3 by Enea Bastianini, Pedro Acosta cut back in to take the corner and was then wiped out by a too-fast Alex Marquez, with Fabio Di Giannantonio also taken down.But Bezzecchi was one of two riders to have selected the medium rear for the race in lieu of the soft, and the choice proved downright disastrous.Third after the start, he had no pace to stay with the leading duo and was swallowed up by Bastianini, as well as Diogo Moreira and Ai Ogura.Moreira had overtaken Ogura while the latter was trying to make his way past Bezzecchi, and then set off after a podium. He reeled in Bastianini towards the end, and both suddenly closed in massively on Martin.Neither made the move, but both Martin and Bastianini fell foul of track limits on the final lap, catching the green paint coming off the kerb at Turn 10 - and thus promoting Moreira to a remarkable second place.The penalties meant Martin is now only seven points ahead of Marquez, with Bezzecchi 45 down on his team-mate.Ogura took fifth place ahead of Bezzecchi, followed by Johann Zarco and Raul Fernandez - who had engaged in a back-and-forth duel through the race.Fabio Quartararo snuck into ninth, fending off Fermin Aldeguer late on and ensuring that all five manufacturers scored in the sprint.The only rider to retire besides the three involved in the opening-lap crash was Pecco Bagnaia, last year's grand prix-and-sprint winner, who ran 13th but came in on the final lap with a shredded rear tyre.1 Marc Marquez (Ducati)2 Diogo Moreira (LCR Honda) +2.754s3 Jorge Martin (Aprilia) +2.466s*4 Enea Bastianini (Tech3 KTM) +2.508s*5 Ai Ogura (Trackhouse Aprilia) +5.992s6 Marco Bezzecchi (Aprilia) +6.984s7 Johann Zarco (LCR Honda) +8.088s8 Raul Fernandez (Trackhouse Aprilia) +8.817s9 Fabio Quartararo (Yamaha) +10.586s10 Fermin Aldeguer (Gresini Ducati) +11.129s11 Luca Marini (Honda) +13.632s12 Franco Morbidelli (VR46 Ducati) +15.209s13 Alex Rins (Yamaha) +19.873s14 Somkiat Chantra (Honda) +19.983s15 Maverick Vinales (Tech3 KTM) +20.469s16 Jack Miller (Pramac Yamaha) +21.894s17 Toprak Razgatlioglu (Pramac Yamaha) +38.442s*18 Brad Binder (KTM) +41.284sRT Pecco Bagnaia (Ducati)DNF Pedro Acosta (KTM)DNF Alex Marquez (Gresini Ducati)DNF Fabio Di Giannantonio (VR46 Ducati)*denotes penalised riders

item.title: What went on in final Sepang F1 practice
item.author: Ben Anderson
item.content:encoded: Formula 1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli set the pace in final practice for F1’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, as Mercedes recovered from its most difficult Friday of 2026 to lead the way with its heavily upgraded car.Deputy team principal Bradley Lord said Mercedes conducted overnight simulator work to figure out why the upgrades had improved medium- and high-speed corner performance but at the expense of the low-speed turns, which he described as a previous strength of the car.And it would seem that work was successful, as Antonelli became the first driver to lap below 1m37 seconds so far this weekend. On his second set of soft tyres he set a 1m36.302s best to end the session fastest.Red Bull continued its strong practice form in FP3, with Max Verstappen second-fastest but almost three tenths down on Antonelli.Verstappen’s team-mate Isack Hadjar backed that up with the third-fastest time. He complained of the recently upgraded RB22 being “so unpredictable” through Turns 1 and 9 early on, before ending the session 0.558s off the pace.George Russell was only fourth in the other Mercedes, six tenths off Antonelli, while the Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton rounded out the top six, seven tenths off the pace and separated by just 0.025s.With track temperatures running in the mid-50s°C, the tyres were only good for a single flying lap and couldn’t produce better laptimes even after several cool-down laps or time in the pits.McLaren struggled to extract performance from the soft compound in FP3 and ended up seventh and eighth, with Lando Norris setting his best lap on the medium (C3) tyre. He was eight tenths off the pace, while team-mate Oscar Piastri was a full second off Antonelli, having only found a tenth of a second going from medium to soft.After a Friday spent solely focused on high-fuel long runs owing to a hefty grid penalty he faces for this race, Franco Colapinto led the way in the midfield for Alpine, 1.6s off the pace, ahead of Arvid Lindblad’s Racing Bulls and the Audi of Gabriel Bortoleto.And Fernando Alonso indicated Aston Martin might be a Q2 threat at Sepang by setting the 12th-fastest time FP3, just over three tenths down on Colapinto’s Alpine and 0.018s up on Pierre Gasly’s.1 Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes) 1m36.302s2 Max Verstappen (Red Bull) +0.278s3 Isack Hadjar (Red Bull) +0.558s4 George Russell (Mercedes) +0.610s5 Charles Leclerc (Ferrari) +0.714s6 Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari) +0.739s7 Lando Norris (McLaren) +0.859s8 Oscar Piastri (McLaren) +1.064s9 Franco Colapinto (Alpine) +1.618s10 Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls) +1.782s11 Gabriel Bortoleto (Audi) +1.902s12 Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin) +1.921s13 Pierre Gasly (Alpine) +1.939s14 Esteban Ocon (Haas) +1.950s15 Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls) +1.964s16 Nico Hulkenberg (Audi) +2.054s17 Ollie Bearman (Haas) +2.390s18 Carlos Sainz (Williams) +2.414s19 Lance Stroll (Aston Martin) +2.509s20 Alex Albon (Williams) +2.747s21 Valtteri Bottas (Cadillac) +3.629s22 Sergio Perez (Cadillac) +3.921s

item.title: MotoGP Japanese GP: Martin edges out Marquez to claim back-to-back pole positions
Martin upsets Marquez to score surprise Motegi pole
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: MotoGP championship leader Jorge Martin sniped Motegi pole position from title rival Marc Marquez after a substantial turnaround from Friday practice.Martin, who was only eighth-fastest on Friday, maximised the final sector on his second Q2 run to jump ahead of Marquez by a tenth, securing the new Motegi pole record in the process.Marquez had held provisional Japanese Grand Prix pole after the opening runs, but couldn't improve on his second Q2 outing - which included a trip into the gravel at Turn 3.Third title contender Marco Bezzecchi took a front-row spot for the briefest of moments in the end, before surrendering it right away to Pedro Acosta, who had used Bezzecchi as reference.Alex Marquez (Gresini Ducati) completed a top five covered by just 0.175s, ahead of Fabio Di Giannantonio (VR46 Ducati), Enea Bastianini (Tech3 KTM), and Q1 graduate Raul Fernandez (Trackhouse Aprilia).LCR team-mates Diogo Moreira and Johann Zarco were next up, Zarco crashing in Q2, while Ai Ogura - who, like team-mate Fernandez, advanced from Q1 - and Fabio Quartararo rounded out the Q2 order.Yellow flags triggered by a fast Brad Binder crash entering the Turns 12-13-14 sequence nearly compromised Fernandez in Q1 and nearly put defending Motegi winner Pecco Bagnaia through into Q2 instead - but Fernandez had enough time to go again and consign Bagnaia to fifth row on the grid.Joining him on that row will be Ducati stablemate Franco Morbidelli and Q1 standout Somkiat Chantra. Chantra, riding as Joan Mir's substitute rider at the factory Honda team, produced a better qualifying result than any of his efforts in his full-time season in 2025 - and outqualified team-mate Luca Marini in the process.It was a disappointing run to 18th on the grid for Fermin Aldeguer, as he outqualified only the returning Maverick Vinales and three Yamahas.1 Jorge Martin (Aprilia) 1m42.371s2 Marc Marquez (Ducati) +0.110s3 Pedro Acosta (KTM) +0.122s4 Marco Bezzecchi (Aprilia) +0.159s5 Alex Marquez (Gresini Ducati) +0.175s6 Fabio Di Giannantonio (VR46 Ducati) +0.257s7 Enea Bastianini (Tech3 KTM) +0.298s8 Raul Fernandez (Trackhouse Aprilia) +0.370s9 Diogo Moreira (LCR Honda) +0.545s10 Johann Zarco (LCR Honda) +0.547s11 Ai Ogura (Trackhouse Aprilia) +0.562s12 Fabio Quartararo (Yamaha) +0.751s13 Pecco Bagnaia (Ducati) +0.123s to Q214 Franco Morbidelli (VR46 Ducati) +0.252s15 Somkiat Chantra (Honda) +0.312s16 Luca Marini (Honda) +0.394s17 Brad Binder (KTM) +0.515s18 Fermin Aldeguer (Gresini Ducati) +0.535s19 Maverick Vinales (Tech3 KTM) +0.721s20 Jack Miller (Pramac Yamaha) +0.927s21 Alex Rins (Yamaha) +1.012s22 Toprak Razgatlioglu (Pramac Yamaha) +1.147s

item.title: USA gets another UCI race as Battenkill returns to pro calendar
item.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: One year after returning to the domestic pro calendar, the Battenkill road race in New York State is back on the UCI calendar after a 13-year absence, giving another boost for professional cycling in North America.The race will run on May 22, 2027, as a UCI 1.2-ranked men's race, two weeks before the Armed Forces Cycling Classic Capitol Cup, also a men's 1.2 race, will be held on June 5.The return of Battenkill follows the revival of the Philadelphia Cycling Classic p/b Amerigas, UCI 1.1-ranked road races for men and women. Together with the Tour of the Gila men's and women's 2.2-ranked stage races, these are the only US events currently listed on the UCI's 2027 road calendar.As of yet, the Gran Premio New York City is not listed on the UCI's calendar, but organisers assured Cyclingnews that the application was submitted for a 1.2-ranked men's event, scheduled for May 16, 2027.Battenkill, formerly known as Tour of the Battenkill, was held as a UCI race twice before, the first time in 2010, when Caleb Fairly soloed to the win ahead of Floyd Landis. Francisco Mancebo won the other edition in 2012. The event continued as a gran fondo in intervening years under different ownership, but the 2027 edition brings it back into the hands of Anthem Sports."Bringing Battenkill back to the UCI calendar has been one of our major goals since returning the event to Cambridge," event director Dieter Drake said. "Battenkill was built around hard, unpredictable racing on beautiful but unforgiving roads. The UCI race gives us an opportunity to bring that experience back to professional riders while also introducing a new generation of cyclists to what makes this event so special."Organisers compare the course to the Belgian classics, where numerous short, steep climbs, narrow roads and unpaved sections favour positioning, tactics and the ability to endure repeated efforts."There isn't one climb where you can say the race will be decided," Drake said. "The entire course makes the selection. Riders are constantly being asked to make decisions - where to position themselves, when to spend energy, how aggressively to ride the dirt and when to attack. That has always been the essence of Battenkill."The 2027 race will be based around the village of Cambridge, with a full weekend of events for amateur racers and recreational riders, and Drake hopes it will become a long-term fixture on the calendar."We aren't trying to reinvent Battenkill," Drake said. "We're trying to preserve what made people remember it. Cambridge, the dirt roads, the farms, the weather, the climbs and the unpredictability are all part of the race. Bringing the UCI event back gives us the opportunity to build on that history rather than replace it."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Evans names Solberg the “danger man” in WRC title fight
Lachlan Morton set to leave EF Education-EasyPost
item.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: Lachlan Morton, one of the most popular riders of the EF Education-EasyPost squad, revealed that he is leaving the team after six seasons with the US outfit. The ultra-endurance specialist told that his victory in the 3-Peaks endurance cyclocross race in Yorkshire last weekend was his "last time pinning on a number with EF".Morton began his career as part of the organisation when it was Garmin-Sharp after racing for the development squad, but turned his focus to pushing his body in long-distance challenges beginning in 2014. He returned to the WorldTour in 2017 and then returned to EF Education in 2019.But the lonely road didn't stop calling, and in 2021 Morton completed the entire Tour de France route - including transfers - solo. It marked the start of a different relationship with the team, completing various long-distance challenges and gravel races instead of racing in the WorldTour.With his time in pink ending, the 34-year-old will continue to perform superhuman feats of endurance around the globe, telling that he has an eye on Pakistan, Papua New Guinea and Ecuador for his future adventures.First, Morton will attempt to follow the Pony Express route - a 3,164-kilometre ride from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California, beginning on Monday, October 5, the EF Education-EasyPost team announced on Friday. The route was used in the 1860s by young riders on horseback who carried mail across Missouri, Kansas, Nebraska, Colorado, Wyoming, Nevada and into California."You start on the plains, essentially, coming across Kansas, then across the basin through Wyoming, into Utah," Morton said in the team's press release. "The real crux is the Nevada section - the stretch from Salt Lake City across to Carson City - because it's incredibly remote and very exposed. There's a lot that could go wrong there, and you're very much on your own. That's probably the hardest part. "Then you cross the Sierra Nevada on the southern side of Lake Tahoe and drop through the foothills, which I know well because I live out there now, and finish in Sacramento."The fastest time on horseback was set in 1861 at seven days, 17 hours, but the route fell out of use after the first telegraph lines were completed and eliminated the need for rapid hand-delivered messages."The way they could get mail across the country at that speed - before there was any railroad connecting it – was revolutionary," Morton said. "The idea of people traversing such massive distances just captured my imagination, especially knowing a lot of that terrain. Think of these big open spaces - huge plains, mountain ranges - and you imagine a slow transition, but with the elevation and the vegetation it's always evolving, and when you're covering big distances you get a really diverse variety of riding. It's a great canvas for adventure. It's existed there for so long, and you feel like you're participating in what the country is all about."Morton is familiar with at least some of the route, having set the fastest time on the Tour Divide from Alberta to New Mexico in 2023, although his time has since been eclipsed.In his Pony Express attempt, Morton will deliver letters along the route just to fully embrace the origins of the route."The appeal for me is the history of it," Morton said. "It's wild to get into that mindset – you're a kid trying to make some money, and there's this opportunity to ride a horse with a mochila full of mail through the night for 75 miles (120 kilometres) flat out, across remote, gnarly terrain that no one else has been crossing. It's quite a courageous thing. It's hard to imagine, and that's why I want to go out there and try to get a better understanding of what that would have been like, and the difficulties they faced doing it over 150 years ago."Just as the riders of old swapped horses to continue at speed, Morton will switch between the Cannondale TopStone gravel bike, his SuperSix lightweight road bike and the Scalpel full-suspension mountain bike."The route I've put together tries to get as close to the original as I could. I'm excited because it'll use all the different disciplines I've raced," Morton said.You can follow Morton's Pony Express ride here.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia.
